How did game developers pack entire games into so little memory twenty five years ago?

I'm not exactly sure, but I believe that most of the space that games take up comes from resources, such as models, textures, sounds and other non-code stuff, as the programming is actually a pretty small part. For example in Sonic The Hedgehog, the "Sega chant at the beginning took up one eighth of the entire cartridge!" So you can only imagine how many gigabytes are spent on all of the high quality graphics and audio put into each AAA game these days.

Old fart here; there are several reasons:

  • Hand-optimized assembly or machine code. Nobody does that anymore
  • No videos or pre-rendered cutscenes
  • Music was MIDI or some sort of tracker using small, crappy samples or chip generated audio
  • 2D, low resolution graphics with a tiny color palette
  • Procedurally generated everything

But most importantly, an almost fanatical focus on resource limitations and optimization. It's a lost art. Well, almost.

Well, this isn't directly related towards game development, but it is software related from about 22 years ago.

A former friend of mine was writing computer BBS software in C++. As he was showing me the code, I recall him mentioning to me a few times how he was removing a lot of unnecessary information from the header files as a way to make his program smaller. Remember, we were dealing with 2400 to 14.4k baud modems at the time. From what he was telling me, mindset amongst programmers at the time was to not create bloat and to streamline and optimize everything.

Well now that emulators have come out and some Roms are sometimes around 3mbs. For example Chrono Trigger. The Rom is around that much.

So I would imagine that, on a duel layered blue ray disc, they could fit a lot of amounts of data, they could potentially make a game so big it could take months to beat, on a scale, and around the same graphics and storywise as an RPG like Chrono Trigger. At least, that's what I would assume.
